claims.text: Total tribo-corrosion degradation in high-entropy alloys is governed by the dynamic balance between protective oxide-film formation and mechanical film removal.
Alloy composition determines the stability and regeneration rate of the protective oxide film.
The proposed high-entropy alloy has a multiphase microstructure.
Cr, Al, and Ti are oxide-forming elements that can contribute to a protective surface film in oxidative environments.
Oxide-film thickness, stability, integrity, and repassivation rate mediate the tribo-corrosion response.
Sliding wear mechanically abrades the passive oxide film.
Removal of the passive film exposes fresh alloy surface that oxidizes in the corrosive environment.
Alloy composition modulates the kinetics of oxide regrowth after mechanical damage.
A stable, rapidly forming oxide layer mitigates corrosion within mechanically damaged regions.
When repassivation is too slow, local corrosion and total degradation increase.
An alloy optimized for oxide-film stability will have a lower corrosion-damage component than a mechanically matched alloy containing less of the key oxide-forming elements.
The optimized alloy may still experience mechanically driven wear.
Rapid oxide-film repair will reduce overall degradation relative to the baseline alloy.
Reducing the content of key oxide-forming elements produces a less stable or more slowly regenerating passive film.
The predicted benefit should hold when oxide regrowth can keep pace with mechanically induced film removal.
Very high contact stress or high chloride concentration can remove or undermine the oxide film too rapidly for the predicted benefit to persist.
